title: Kedoshim: don't stand idly by (Leviticus 19:16)
hookLine: "neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbor"

lines: A FALL ON A BUSY PLATFORM.
cards: A person falls on a busy train platform. Plenty of people see it, and each one waits, half-sure somebody else will step forward.
Someone is being piled on in a group chat, and the messages get read, one by one, and nobody types a thing. Psychologists call this kind of waiting the bystander effect.
Leviticus 19 put the problem into a single verse, long before anyone gave it a name.

teach.b: The verse, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people; neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD."
Notice the pairing: don't spread stories, and don't stay out of it. Talk too much, or do too little: both fail a neighbor.
Literally, the Hebrew says: do not stand upon your neighbor's blood. Standing still while someone bleeds. The translators added idly, and it fits.
The Talmud asks where we learn that if you see someone drowning, or dragged off by a wild animal, or attacked by robbers, you are obligated to save them. The answer: from this verse.
And it goes further: if you can't save them yourself, you must hire others to help. Maimonides rules that anyone who could save a life and doesn't has broken this commandment.
Being present and doing nothing is not neutral.
Look back at the week. Azazel carried the wrongs away. Ask the person first.
Then Kedoshim: holiness for everyone, the corners of the field, no stumbling block, and now this. The Kedoshim days each hand an ordinary person a job. Not the priest.
You, on the platform, in the group chat, at the scene.

how: Jewish law treats rescuing someone in danger as a positive duty, drawn from Leviticus 19:16, and the verse is often cited in Jewish teaching about speaking up for people in danger or being harmed.

o: holy ones, the portion this week ends on
a talebearer spreading stories among the people
the bystander who stands by a neighbor's blood

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: going up and down with stories
drowning, beasts or robbers: save them

s: in Jewish law, watching without helping is neutral
the Talmud and Maimonides count failing to save as breaking this commandment.
the same verse also forbids talebearing
don't spread stories, and don't stand idly by.
the duty to rescue applies only if you can do it yourself
the Talmud says if you can't, you must hire others to help.

games.q: you see someone struggling in the river. you can't swim. what does the Talmud say you must do?
o: get or pay others to save them.
games.why: the Talmud says you must hire others to help if you can't do it yourself. standing by isn't an option.

practice: Think of a place where you've been a bystander lately: a coworker everyone talks over, a neighbor who seems to be struggling, a thread where someone's getting piled on. Picture yourself being the one who does something.
Not heroic: a question, a call, a message, a word in a meeting.

wordCard.voice: Kedoshim. The portion that says you may not stand idly by your neighbor's blood: if you can help, you must.

orig.note: Hebrew: "do not stand upon your neighbor's blood" (Leviticus 19:16).

carryVoice: Your line: don't stand idly by. Watching is never quite neutral. Another week of Leviticus, done.
